title: Make a Decision
content:
What problem does this solve?
So far every line runs whenever Python reaches it. An if/else lets the program choose one path based on a True-or-False question.

Start with the question
  count = 6
  print(count >= 5)
The comparison count >= 5 produces either True or False.

Use the result to choose behavior
  score = 3
  if score >= 5:
      print("ready")
  else:
      print("wait")
Python checks the if condition. If it is True, the indented if block runs. Otherwise the else block runs. Exactly one branch runs in this two-path structure.

Boundary words matter
'5 or more' means >= 5. The value 5 belongs on the ready side. Small words such as 'or more' and 'less than' determine the comparison you need.
concepts: A comparison produces True or False
if runs its indented block when the condition is True
else runs when the if condition is False
= stores a value; == compares two values
Boundary wording determines whether a threshold value is included

examples.title: A comparison
examples.explanation: 6 is at least 5, so the comparison produces True.

examples.title: Two paths
examples.explanation: 3 is not at least 5, so the else branch runs.

examples.title: Abandoned camp
examples.explanation: The decision is driven by the stored counts.

common_mistakes: Using = inside a condition when you mean ==
Forgetting the colon after if or else
Lining up code incorrectly so it is outside the intended branch
Using > when the rule says 'or more' and should include the boundary

exercises.title: Read a comparison
hints: Translate >= as 'greater than or equal to.'
Ask whether 6 is greater than or equal to 5.
The comparison is True.

exercises.title: Choose the branch
hints: Evaluate score >= 5 before choosing a branch.
3 >= 5 is False, so Python skips the if block.
The else branch prints wait.

exercises.title: Write the comparison
exercises.prompt: Change the condition so a value of 10 or more prints high. Keep the starter value 12. The output should be exactly high.
hints: The rule includes 10 itself.
Use a comparison that means 'greater than or equal to 10.'
Change the condition to value >= 10.

tests.message: Compare value with an inclusive >= boundary.

exercises.title: Which side owns 5?
exercises.prompt: The rule is: '5 or more is ready.' Which comparison matches that rule?
hints: Pay attention to the words 'or more.'
The boundary value 5 must count as ready.
Choose score >= 5.
exercises.success_message: Correct. >= includes the boundary value itself.

exercises.title: Compare instead of assign
exercises.prompt: Repair the condition so Python compares status to the text "ready". The output should be exactly go.
hints: The first = already stored a value in status. Inside the if, you need a True-or-False comparison.
Python uses == to ask whether two values are equal.
Change the condition to if status == "ready":

exercises.title: Empty or not
exercises.prompt: The starter variable count is supplied. Print empty when count == 0. Otherwise print has items. Keep the starter value at 0 while checking this exercise.
hints: The decision asks one yes-or-no question about count.
Compare count with 0 using ==, then give the other case to else.
Use if count == 0: print("empty") else: print("has items").

exercises.title: The Abandoned Camp
exercises.prompt:
Given the supplied expedition data, print exactly one status line.

Rule:
- if bedrolls < registered: Expedition 17: INVESTIGATE
- otherwise: Expedition 17: CLEAR

Use the variables, one if/else, and an f-string. Do not hardcode the expedition number into both possible output lines.
exercises.starter_code:
expedition = 17
registered = 4
bedrolls = 3

# Decide the camp status and print one line
exercises.reference_solution:
expedition = 17
registered = 4
bedrolls = 3

if bedrolls < registered:
    print(f"Expedition {expedition}: INVESTIGATE")
else:
    print(f"Expedition {expedition}: CLEAR")
hints: First decide what fact separates the two outcomes: compare bedrolls with registered.
Put the < comparison in if, then use else for the equal-or-greater case. Build each output line from expedition with an f-string.
Use if bedrolls < registered: print(f"Expedition {expedition}: INVESTIGATE") else: print(f"Expedition {expedition}: CLEAR").
exercises.success_message: The program now chooses its report from the data instead of always printing the same status.
